opus-5.5.text:
Ha, "look down on" might be a bit strong, but I'll admit there was some of that attitude, and I think it came from a particular culture.

At MIT, especially in the physics department and in Max Tegmark's group, the mindset was: we want to *understand* things. In physics you don't stop at a model that fits the data; you want the underlying principles, the conservation laws, the simple equations behind complicated phenomena. When we looked at deep learning, it seemed like a huge, messy empirical system nobody really understood. So the natural physicist's instinct was that if we could find the "laws" of neural networks, like how representations form, why grokking happens, and what the network is actually computing inside, that would be more fundamental and longer-lasting than any single model.

From that angle, industry looked like it was doing engineering, not science. Scale up the model, add more data, more GPUs, tune things until the benchmark goes up. There was a feeling of, "That works, but you don't know *why* it works, and isn't the 'why' the interesting part?" I think many of us felt that was a less intellectually serious path, maybe even a bit brute-force.

Looking back, I think that view was partly right and partly naive. It was right that understanding matters. Interpretability, mechanistic understanding, and something like a physics of AI are still important, and probably more important now that these systems are so powerful. But it was naive to underestimate how much *knowledge* was actually being generated by scaling. Scaling laws themselves are a very physics-like discovery: empirical regularities spanning orders of magnitude. And industry was running experiments at a scale academia simply couldn't touch. Phenomena only show up at that scale, so if you want to do the physics of AI, in some sense the "experimental apparatus" lives in industry.

So my attitude has shifted. I now think of it less as science versus engineering and more like the relationship between experimentalists and theorists in physics. The large labs are building the particle accelerators, and people like me are trying to come up with the theory to explain what comes out. You need both, and frankly the theorists had been a bit arrogant about it.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I should start by saying "look down" is maybe too strong, but it's not completely wrong either. There was a certain attitude, and I absorbed it.

When I came to MIT to work with Max Tegmark, the whole premise of our group was that neural networks are physical systems. They have dynamics, they have conserved quantities, they have phase transitions. So the natural belief is: if you really understand the physics, you can derive how these things work from first principles, and then you don't need to grope around in the dark. You don't need to just scale up and see what happens. That was the dream. Grokking, neural scaling laws, KAN, these all came out of that mindset of "let's find the mechanism."

And when you hold that belief, it's very easy to look at industry and think, these people are just doing alchemy. They're mixing things in a pot, adding more compute, tweaking hyperparameters, and they don't know why anything works. We're the chemists, they're the alchemists. There was definitely a kind of intellectual pride in that. Like, we're doing the real science and they're doing engineering.

But I think in the last couple of years that attitude got humbled, at least for me. Because the alchemists kept producing gold. The scaling hypothesis worked much better than any of our elegant theories predicted. And a lot of the beautiful phenomena we studied, like grokking, turned out to be very hard to connect to what actually matters at frontier scale. So I had to ask myself, am I understanding the thing, or am I understanding a toy version of the thing?

So now my view is more balanced. Physics gives you taste, it gives you a way to ask good questions, it gives you intuition about what should be universal. But industry has the data, the compute, and honestly the empirical feedback loop that keeps you honest. I don't think I looked down on them so much as I underestimated how much you can learn by just building the thing at scale.

astra-6.text: At the time, I took the idea of a “physics of AI” to mean that there were deep principles waiting to be discovered, and that finding them was the most important work. From that perspective, it was easy to dismiss industry as just scaling models, collecting more data, and doing engineering. I confused searching for fundamental explanations with being intellectually superior. But that’s a false distinction: making something work can reveal phenomena that your theory hasn’t even thought to explain.
